lesson.title: VXLAN: Stretching Layer 2 Across the Data Center
lesson.summary: VXLAN is a standardized overlay encapsulation protocol that tunnels Ethernet frames inside UDP packets, letting cloud data centers extend isolated virtual layer 2 networks across a routed layer 3 physical fabric at large scale.
lesson.body:
Overlay networks solve a general problem: build a virtual topology on top of physical infrastructure using encapsulation. VXLAN, short for Virtual Extensible LAN, is a specific, standardized way of doing that, purpose built for a problem that shows up constantly in modern cloud data centers, stretching layer 2, Ethernet, connectivity across infrastructure that is fundamentally routed at layer 3.

Traditional VLANs, the mechanism most networks have long used to create isolated layer 2 segments, use a 12 bit tag, which allows for only 4094 usable VLAN IDs. That ceiling was fine for a single enterprise network, but it is far too small for a large multi tenant cloud data center that might need to give thousands of separate customers, each running many virtual machines, their own isolated logical network. VLANs also do not extend cleanly across the layer 3 routed fabrics that large data centers use for scalability and resilience, since a VLAN is inherently a layer 2 construct.

VXLAN addresses both problems. It encapsulates an entire Ethernet frame, headers and all, inside a UDP packet, which can then be routed normally across an ordinary layer 3 IP network. Instead of a 12 bit VLAN tag, VXLAN uses a 24 bit VXLAN Network Identifier, or VNI, which supports over 16 million distinct logical segments, comfortably enough for large scale multi tenant environments. The encapsulation and decapsulation happen at devices called VTEPs, VXLAN Tunnel Endpoints, which are commonly implemented in hypervisor virtual switches or in top of rack physical switches.

A concrete data center scenario shows why this matters. Imagine a cloud provider running many tenants' virtual machines across a large fleet of physical servers, where a single tenant's VMs might land on physical hosts in different racks, connected only by a routed layer 3 fabric. That tenant still expects their VMs to behave as though they are on one shared layer 2 network, able to reach each other directly the way machines on the same physical LAN would. VXLAN makes this possible: the tenant's VMs are assigned a shared VNI, and when one VM sends a frame to another, the sending host's VTEP encapsulates that Ethernet frame in a UDP packet addressed to the destination host's VTEP. The physical network fabric in between just sees ordinary IP traffic between two server addresses and routes it accordingly, with no awareness that it is actually carrying an isolated tenant's private layer 2 traffic. This pattern, sometimes deployed together with SDN controllers that manage VTEP configuration and VNI assignment across the fabric, is a common way that virtual networks are actually built inside large cloud and enterprise data centers today.
